lines.text: The word RAM lets you count steps, and a recursive algorithm hands you that count as a recurrence.
This is how to read the answer.
Take the vector of a million keys, and three recursive procedures on it. Merge sort. Binary search. And median of medians.
Each one's count is an equation that defines T of n through T at smaller sizes.
Two of them recurse twice. One of those two is linear, and the other is not.
By the end, you will read all three off their trees.
Draw the recurrence as what it is... a tree of calls.
Each node does its own work, then calls itself twice on halves.
A level is some number of nodes, all of one size, so its total is that number times the work of one.
For merge sort on sixty four keys, every level totals sixty four.
Seven levels, so add up the column. That is four hundred and forty eight in all.
Same kind of tree, new recurrence. Every call now makes eight calls on half the keys, and does n squared work itself.
The root alone does four thousand and ninety six units of work. The calls at the bottom are on one key, and do one unit each.
What do the calls at the bottom add up to?
The bottom level totals two to the power eighteen.
Eight calls per node, six levels down... that is a lot of leaves, each doing one unit.
The column doubles at every level, so the bottom row is sixty four times the root.
That leaf count has a name. The watershed. When the leaves win, the answer is the watershed itself.
The Master theorem is nothing but three shapes the column can take.
Compare one level with the next.
Smaller by a constant factor... the column shrinks, and the root is the answer.
Equal... every level ties, so you multiply by the number of levels. That is the log.
Larger by a constant factor... the leaves win.
A geometric series is a constant times its largest term. That is the whole proof.
The textbook statement compares f of n with the watershed.
Polynomially smaller, case one. The leaves win.
The same size, case two. A tie, with one more log.
Polynomially larger, case three, and the root wins... but only if a regularity condition holds, so the column really shrinks.
For a simple power it holds by itself. The fraction here is two over four, which is one half.
Binary search is case two, with a watershed of one. The log comes from the depth alone.
The three cases are not exhaustive.
Here f is n log n. It is above the watershed, but not by any power of n, and it is not the same size either.
The column does shrink, yet the ratio of nearby levels creeps up towards one.
So no constant below one fits, and none of the three cases applies.
A log power patches this one. The extended case two allows the same size, up to a log power.
The gap that remains is from below. The general theorem, in a moment, covers it. Recursion trees cover the rest.
Median of medians recurses on two different sizes... a fifth, and seven tenths.
The Master theorem has one split factor. It cannot take this.
The tree still can. A fifth plus seven tenths is nine tenths.
Each level now totals nine tenths of the level above, so the work shrinks by the same factor.
The root dominates. The total stays under ten times n. Linear.
Now change the groups. Groups of three give T of n over three, plus T of two n over three, plus n.
Still linear?
No. A third plus two thirds is exactly one.
So every full level adds back up to n, and the levels run about log n deep.
That is n log n. This analysis can no longer show linear time.
The sum of the fractions decides. Below one, the column shrinks. At exactly one, it ties.
The general theorem turns that sum into an exponent.
Find the one number p where the fractions, each raised to the power p, add up to one.
For selection, p is about zero point eight four.
With f equal to n, the integral grows like n to the one minus p, and n to the p times that is just n. Linear.
The Master theorem is the one term case. And floors, ceilings and plus six are absorbed by small perturbations.
Now the proof side, substitution. Guess, then prove by induction.
Merge sort, guess T of n is at most c times n.
The step gives... c times n, plus n.
What has this proved?
Nothing. The step has to come back to exactly c times n, and c times n plus n is larger, for any c.
The constant may not grow. You cannot induct over big O.
The guess was simply wrong. The real ratio climbs by three, every time n grows eight times.
A second trap. Here the guess is right.
Counting merge sort's calls, the Master theorem says linear, and the counts say two n minus one.
But the induction still fails by the plus one.
Subtract a lower order term. Take the guess and subtract a constant. The step then closes, as soon as that constant is at least one.
A stronger hypothesis is easier to prove.
Back to the problem.
Merge sort doubles, but every level costs n. A tie. N log n.
Binary search never doubles, and costs one per level. Log n.
Median of medians doubles, but each level costs nine tenths of the last. The root wins. Linear.
At a million keys, with the constant in each recurrence set to one, those solve to about twenty one million units of work, twenty probes, and eight point eight million units.
Next, what every algorithm must pay.
Prove it, one of three.
T of n equals seven T of n over two, plus n squared.
Which end of the column wins?
The leaves. The watershed is n to the log base two of seven, about n to the two point eight one.
With seven calls instead of eight, the exponent falls from three to two point eight one.
Prove it, two of three.
T of n equals two T of n over two, plus n over log n.
A colleague applies case two, and writes n log n. Right?
No case applies. This f sits below the watershed by only a log factor.
The general theorem gives n log log n.
The tree agrees. The levels add up like a harmonic series.
Prove it, three of three.
T of n equals four T of n over two, plus n. The Master theorem says n squared.
Your induction with a constant times n squared ends at that, plus n. What now?
Strengthen the guess. A bigger constant never helps, because the plus n sits outside it.
Subtract a linear term, and the step closes. The theorem was right.
A recurrence bounds what one algorithm costs. Next, how to prove that no algorithm can do better.
